cards.front: Recall a key point about Pure Substances And Formulations
cards.back: In everyday language, "pure" means something that is free from contamination. In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound that contains only one type of atom or one type of molecule throughout.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Pure Substances And Formulations
cards.back: A pure substance has a sharp, specific melting point and a sharp, specific boiling point . These fixed points can be used to identify the substance and confirm its purity.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Pure Substances And Formulations
cards.back: The melting point and boiling point of a substance can be used to determine whether it is pure. A pure substance melts and boils at a single, fixed temperature. A mixture melts and boils over a range of temperatures .

cards.front: Recall a key point about Pure Substances And Formulations
cards.back: Impurities lower the melting point of a substance and raise the boiling point. The greater the amount of impurity, the wider the melting or boiling range.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Pure Substances And Formulations
cards.back: A formulation is a mixture that has been designed as a useful product. It is made by mixing specific quantities of different substances (components) in carefully measured proportions so that the product meets its required purpose.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Pure Substances And Formulations
cards.back: Each component in a formulation has a specific function. Changing the proportions of the components changes the properties and performance of the product.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Pure Substances And Formulations
cards.back: Formulations are not pure substances. They are carefully designed mixtures where each component plays a specific role. The ratio of each component is critical to the performance and safety of the product.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Pure Substances And Formulations
cards.back: To test whether a substance is pure, measure its melting point or boiling point and compare it to known data for the pure substance: If the measured value matches the reference value exactly, the substance is likely pure. If the substance melts or boils over a range of temperatures, it is a mixture. If the melting point is lower than expected, impurities are present.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Pure Substances And Formulations
cards.back: In everyday language, "pure" often means "nothing added" or "natural". For example, "pure orange juice" means no added sugar or water, but it is still a mixture of many chemical compounds. In chemistry, this orange juice is not a pure substance.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Pure Substances And Formulations
cards.back: Since formulations are mixtures, their components can be separated by physical methods. The choice of method depends on the type of mixture:
Single element or compound (e.g. Two or more substances combined)
Sharp, fixed temperature (e.g. Melts over a range of temperatures)
Sharp, fixed temperature (e.g. Boils over a range of temperatures)

cards.front: What does Effect of impurities mean?
cards.back: No impurities present (e.g. Impurities lower melting point and raise boiling point)
Cannot be separated by physical means (e.g. Can be separated by physical methods (filtration, distillation, chromatography))
